Tuesday. Stayed late at the bakery again because the new oven kept tripping the breaker. Got home at nine to find Marcus had already put the kids to bed and left a plate of cold pasta for me. I felt guilty and grateful at once. Little Odette had drawn me a picture of our house with a giant sun on it. I taped it above the kettle. Tomorrow I'm going to leave on time, even if the croissants burn. Some things are more important than perfect pastry.

March 3rd. Mum called this morning while I was in the middle of inventory at the hardware store. She wanted to know if I'd be home for Easter. I said I'd try, but honestly, Gerald has me on the schedule every weekend through April. I hate how tired her voice sounded. After my shift I drove past her street just to look at the porch light. Didn't stop in. I'll ring her tomorrow and ask for the lemon cake recipe, which is really just an excuse to talk longer.

Friday night, finally. Today was my first full day back at the clinic since Dad's surgery. Everyone was kind, which somehow made it harder. Priya covered my patients without being asked and left a sticky note saying 'You've got this.' I cried in the supply closet for two minutes, then washed my face and went back out. Dad is walking to the mailbox now. My sister sent a photo of him giving a thumbs-up. I kept it on my phone all shift.

Sunday evening. I told my boss, Mr. Okafor, that I need to cut my hours to be home when Tomas gets out of school. My hands were shaking the whole conversation. He paused, then said he'd see what he could do. Now I'm sitting at the kitchen table doing budget math, and it's tight, but not impossible. Tomas asked what I was writing. I told him, 'Just figuring out how to see you more.' He shrugged and said, 'Cool,' then hugged me anyway.

Dear diary, the farm auction is next week and nobody at supper said a word about it. Pa just kept cutting his potatoes into smaller and smaller pieces. I've worked these fields since I was twelve, and I can't picture mornings without the cows. Brother Wendell says he'll take a job at the cannery in town. I might do the same. Tonight I walked the fence line alone and said goodbye to each post, feeling a little foolish, but I did it anyway.

Wednesday. My daughter Lina started her first job today, scooping ice cream at the pier. She came home smelling like waffle cones and announced she'd earned eleven dollars in tips. I remember my own first job washing dishes at my uncle's diner, how proud I felt holding that first crumpled paycheck. I didn't tell her all that. I just made her tea and let her talk. Watching her grow up feels like losing something and gaining something in the same breath.

October 12. The warehouse was freezing again, and my back aches in that familiar way. Fourteen years of lifting boxes. Still, tonight at dinner my husband Dev laughed so hard at something our son said that milk came out of his nose, and everything felt lighter. We're saving for a trip to the coast next summer. I keep a jar on the dresser, and tonight I dropped in twenty dollars from overtime. It's slow, but the jar is filling up.

Late. Can't sleep. The restaurant was slammed tonight, and I burned my wrist on a sheet pan, but that's not what's keeping me up. My grandmother's eightieth birthday is Saturday, and I promised I'd cook her old mole recipe. I never learned it properly. I only remember her stirring and humming. I called Tía Rosa after closing, and she dictated half of it from memory. I wrote it all on the back of an order ticket. Maybe it'll taste like home.

Thursday, lunch break, scribbling in the car. My teaching assistant job ends in June, and I still haven't told Annika, my wife. Every time I try, she's glowing about the new garden she wants to plant. I don't want to dampen it. But keeping this secret feels like carrying a stone in my coat. Tonight I'll tell her over dinner, before I lose my nerve. Whatever happens, we've figured things out before, and I trust we will again.

Saturday. Spent the morning at the print shop and the afternoon at my son's soccer game, rushing between both with ink still under my fingernails. He missed a goal by an inch, and I cheered anyway. On the sideline, another dad asked how I manage it all. I laughed and said I don't, really. I just show up, a bit late and a bit messy. Afterwards, Ben and I got ice cream, and he leaned his head on my arm.

The summer I turned seven, my grandfather let me steer his rusty green tractor across the back field in Ohio. I sat on a folded feed sack so I could see over the wheel, and he walked beside me, one hand on the fender. Dust coated my teeth. When I finally drove it straight to the fence line, he whistled through his gap tooth and called me his foreman. I have won awards since then, but nothing has ever made me feel as tall as that crooked row of flattened clover.

We lived above my mother's laundry in Karachi, and the whole apartment smelled of starch and hot steam. As a girl, I would fall asleep to the thump of the pressing machine downstairs. Sometimes she sent me down with tea for the workers, and they let me fold handkerchiefs into tiny swans. I thought everyone's mother ran a kingdom of white sheets. Only years later did I understand how tired her hands were, and how she hid it by humming whenever I walked in.

I was nine when we moved from Glasgow to a farm in Manitoba, and I cried the entire first week. Nothing had edges there; the sky just kept going. My brother and I built a fort from hay bales and swore we would run away home. We never did. By October I had learned to milk a cow, and by Christmas I couldn't remember the sound of the city buses. I still miss those buses sometimes, though, which surprises me.

My childhood bedroom had one window facing a brick wall, but I decided it was an ocean view. Every morning I told my little sister that the bricks were waves holding still just for us. She believed me completely. We would salute passing ships, which were really pigeons. Our father, a night-shift baker, would come home smelling of bread and play along, pointing out a whale near the drainpipe. I think of that wall whenever someone tells me imagination costs money.

When I was six, I lost my front tooth in an apple at my aunt's wedding in Lagos. I remember panicking because everyone was dancing and nobody noticed my tragedy. Then my uncle scooped me onto his shoulders, tucked the tooth into his breast pocket, and promised the tooth fairy knew the address. I danced above the crowd with a bleeding grin, sticky with jollof rice and joy. That night, under my pillow, I found a coin and a tiny folded note in his handwriting.

Every Sunday my father took me fishing at a muddy pond outside Tallinn, though we almost never caught anything. I didn't mind. He brought a thermos of sweet tea and a paper bag of sunflower seeds, and we spat the shells into the reeds like competitors. He rarely spoke much at home, but at the pond he told me stories about his own boyhood and the winter he skated to school. I think the fish were just an excuse for him to talk.

I was the kid who hid under the porch during thunderstorms in Georgia. My grandmother knew exactly where I was but pretended not to, calling out, "Wonder where that child has got to?" while rain hammered the steps. Eventually she'd slide a biscuit with honey through the lattice. I'd eat it in the damp dark, listening to her humming above me. Now, whenever lightning cracks, I smell woodsmoke and butter, and I feel strangely safe, as if someone is still pretending not to see me.

At eight, I decided to become a famous detective and spent a whole summer investigating the disappearance of our neighbor's cat in Osaka. I kept a notebook, interviewed the greengrocer, and dusted the garden gate for fingerprints with flour. The cat turned up on day twelve, asleep in our own shed with three kittens. I felt oddly betrayed. My mother laughed so hard she had to sit down, then helped me write a final report, which I still keep in a drawer.

The winter of 1974, our power went out for five days in Leeds, and my parents turned it into an adventure. We cooked sausages over a candle-lit grate and slept in one big pile of coats in the front room. My father told ghost stories using a torch under his chin, badly. I remember feeling the house shrink around us into something warm and small. Years later, with every light on and every screen glowing, I would trade it all for that dark.

I learned to swim in a cold mountain river in Peru, pushed gently by my older cousin Rosa. She held my belly with two fingers and told me the water wanted to carry me if I would let it. I swallowed half the river, coughing and furious. Then suddenly her fingers were gone, and I was floating, staring at the enormous blue, and she was cheering from the rocks. I have never trusted anything as completely since.

So I started growing tomatoes about six years ago, mostly because my neighbor Hal kept bragging about his. Now I've got eleven varieties on the back porch, and honestly, I think store-bought ones taste like wet paper. People say gardening is relaxing, but I get anxious every time the forecast mentions hail. Still, there's nothing like biting into a warm Cherokee Purple straight off the vine. I'd tell anyone to try it, even if you only have a windowsill.

Okay, here's my hot take: vinyl records aren't actually better than streaming. There, I said it. I own about three hundred of them, I love flipping them over, and I adore the cover art. But the sound? Half the time it's pops and warps. What I really love is the ritual, slowing down and listening to one album all the way through. That's the real magic, and you could do it with any format if you had the patience.

My grandmother taught me to knit when I was nine, and I hated it. Fast forward thirty years, and I'm the woman on the bus making socks. Marguerite would laugh if she saw me. I knit through meetings, through movies, through my sister's long phone calls. People ask if it's boring. No! It's the only time my brain goes quiet. Last winter I finished a blanket with four thousand stitches in it, and I cried a little.

I'll be honest, I think fishing is ninety percent sitting and ten percent lying about it afterward. My dad took me to Lake Corrin every August, and we hardly ever caught anything bigger than a sock. But I loved those mornings, the thermos of cocoa, the mist on the water. Now I take my own kid. She complains constantly, and she's also the one who always wants to go back. I figure that's a pretty good sign.

People look at me funny when I say I play chess in the park every Sunday, as if it's an old man's game. Well, I'm twenty-six, and I've lost to a retired bus driver named Dmitri more times than I can count. He just smiles. I've decided losing is the hobby. Every defeat teaches me something, and I come home with a notebook full of mistakes I won't repeat. Okay, I'll probably repeat a few.

Let me tell you why I think everyone should learn to bake bread. It's cheap, it's forgiving, and your whole apartment smells like heaven. I started during lockdown with a sad little jar of sourdough starter I named Gerald. He's still alive, which is more than I can say for my houseplants. Some loaves come out like bricks, sure. But the good ones? I stand in my kitchen and tear off the heel while it's still steaming. Worth every failure.

I run, but I'm slow, and I've made peace with that. For years I thought I needed to be fast to call myself a runner, which is nonsense. Now I jog the river path at six every morning, nod to the same dog walkers, and listen to podcasts about ancient Rome. My knees complain, my lungs complain, and yet I feel almost smug by seven. Nobody's timing me. That's the whole point, really.

I collect old postcards, the ones with handwriting on the back. My wife thinks it's strange, reading strangers' messages, but I find them wonderful. 'Weather dreadful, aunt Pearl insufferable, wish you were here.' That's from 1936, Brighton. I've got nearly nine hundred now, stacked in shoeboxes under the bed. I don't think of it as snooping. I think of it as keeping small voices from disappearing, one stamp at a time.

Honestly, I think video games get a bad reputation. I've been playing since I was seven, and the stories in some of them beat most movies I've seen. Last month I finished a game about a lighthouse keeper, and I sat there in silence for ten minutes afterward. My mom still asks when I'll 'grow out of it.' I tell her never. It's like asking someone when they'll grow out of reading novels, you know?

Birdwatching started as a joke. My roommate Teodora bought me binoculars for my birthday, and I rolled my eyes. Then one morning a bright yellow warbler landed on our fire escape, and that was it, I was hooked. Now I keep a little list, and I'm up to ninety-four species. I wake early on weekends and walk to the marsh with my coffee. It's strange how much calmer the city feels once you start looking up.

Dear Margaret, the move to Tucson has been harder than I admitted on the phone. The heat sits on the house like a lid, and I miss our Sunday walks along the canal. But yesterday a neighbor left a basket of lemons on my porch, no note, nothing. I cried a little, then made lemonade for the first time in years. Please come in October if you can. I'll air out the spare room and buy the awful biscuits you like. Write soon. All my love, Eleanor

Hey Danny, sorry I've gone quiet. Work ate March alive. I'm doing night shifts at the bakery now, which means I flip my whole day around and see nobody but flour. Honestly, I kind of like it. The streets are empty at four a.m., and the first loaf out of the oven is better than any paycheck. Save me a weekend in May? I'll bring bread, and you bring that terrible board game you keep insisting is fun. Miss you, man. Tomas

I still hear your voice telling me to eat properly, so I do, mostly. I'll visit during the break. Kiss Grandpa for me. Your Lucia

Maybe we could go to the lake this summer, the three of us, you, me, and the hat. Write back when you can. Your brother, Walter

I'll call Sunday after I've settled into the flat. Thank you for always believing in me. Love, Anjali

Maybe you can talk sense into him at Christmas. We'll light the stove in your old room. Come home when you can. Your friend always, Beth
